messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 52-year-old school principal who had worked for years in the same public middle school, a job he once described as busy but predictable, until he was assaulted late one afternoon on campus. The building had mostly emptied out after dismissal. He had stayed behind for a parent meeting and was walking from his office toward a side exit when a man confronted him in a dim stretch of hallway near a maintenance alcove. David remembers the suddenness of it more than a clear sequence: the flash of movement, the man stepping too close, the shock of being shoved back and pinned awkwardly against the wall. Even now, when the memory comes up, his body seems to take over before his mind does; his shoulders tense and draw inward, and he feels himself fixed again in that trapped position, as if the assault is happening in his muscles rather than in the past.

In the days after, what unsettled him was how unevenly the event stayed with him. If someone asked him to explain exactly what happened from beginning to end, he found himself struggling. He could not easily call up the whole memory on purpose, and this left him feeling embarrassed and frustrated, especially as an educator used to being organized and articulate. But the memory did not stay away. Instead, it returned in a repetitive, involuntary way, “like a film,” as he put it, running through the same fragments over and over: the hallway, the man’s proximity, the instant of being cornered. Those replays did not feel like recollection in the ordinary sense. They seemed to seize him, and with them came the physical impression of being forced back into the same posture he had been in during the assault.

Over the following months, those looping, bodily memories began to shape the way David moved through his days at school. Entering the auditorium for an assembly, walking into a classroom observation, stepping into the district office for a meeting, he would immediately scan for exits before he took in anything else. In his own building, where he was supposed to project steadiness, his eyes went first to doorways, blind corners, heavy objects on desks, and anything that might serve as a weapon if someone came at him again. A metal stapler, a pair of scissors in the front office, a fire extinguisher mounted by a door: these caught his attention automatically. The repeated film-like returns of the assault, along with the sensation of his body being put back into that pinned position, made the threat feel current rather than over, and he had come to believe that staying alert in this way was the only reason he might not be caught off guard a second time.

This was most obvious in the places that should have felt most familiar. During crowded parent nights, David positioned himself where he could see the main doors. In staff meetings he took seats with a clear path out. If a visitor stepped unexpectedly into the office doorway, he startled so sharply that he felt humiliated afterward, sometimes covering it by pretending he had simply been distracted. The startle itself would often be followed by a quick sweep of the room—who was near him, what was in their hands, where he could move if he needed to. Because he could not reliably summon the memory deliberately, each uninvited replay seemed to arrive with its own authority, convincing him again that danger could erupt without warning. The more the assault returned in that repetitive, bodily way, the more he monitored his surroundings as if vigilance were part of his job.

His wife has noticed that he now studies restaurants the same way, pausing at the entrance and choosing seats based on escape routes rather than comfort. David does not describe this as fear in a simple sense. It feels to him like necessity, like good judgment learned the hard way. At the same time, he is exhausted by how little rest his mind allows him. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent incident at school when a student dropped a metal binder near him in a hallway; he jolted so violently that several students stared, and he spent the next hour replaying the assault in fragments while trying to carry on with his day. He was shaken not only by the reaction but by the realization that the school he leads now feels organized around possible danger. What frightens him most is that this may be permanent—that he will keep living as if every room needs an escape plan, and that the memory will go on finding him even when he cannot find it himself.
